agent_notes: qirbām ('their inward part') is a famous crux. Ibn Ezra reports the reading 'their graves' (qibrām, with the letters swapped); the Septuagint and Syriac are commonly cited for it (not in the packet, so not cited in sources). I follow the Masoretic text and keep 'their inner thought' in the dramatic layer, with the alternative in the commentary. BBE's 'the place of the dead is their house' follows the emended reading. Also, the Hebrew has 'houses' (bāttêmô, an archaic suffix) in the first line and 'dwelling places' in the second.

agent_notes: כסל has two homographs: 'folly' (Eccl 7:25; Rashi, Radak, Meiri here) and 'confidence, trust' (Job 8:14; 31:24; Ps 78:7). The lines are plausibly 'this is the way of those whose trust is in themselves'. I give 'folly' in the layers and mention the other sense in a note. BBE ('silver … gold') reflects a different reading and is not followed.
ירצו here is read as 'approve, delight in' (all five English versions; Ibn Ezra, Radak). Rashi takes it as 'speak, recite'. 'After them' is read as 'those who come after them'.

Request addressed: no Egypt and no Mot material; the commentary rests on the Hebrew and the packet's commentators. The note on וְצוּרָם no longer says anything about the age of the commentators' readings against the Masoretic note.

Hard verse; the five English versions split. KJV/Webster read שתו as 'are laid', ASV as 'are appointed', YLT as 'have set themselves' (Radak allows both), BBE rewrites the verse. I kept the passive-or-reflexive ambiguity in the literal layer ('they are set') and chose the passive in the dramatic layer. STEPBible glosses 'they ruled' for וַיִּרְדּוּ; I glossed it 'and they rule' since the verb is a wayyiqtol continuing a present scene.

מִזְּבֻל לוֹ is the crux of the verse's end. I follow Rashi's first reading (away from having a dwelling) in the literal layer, 'from a lofty abode to it', and leave the final לוֹ open; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David differ on whether the dwelling is the man's or Sheol's. The Hebrew form צוּרָם is glossed 'their form' with Ibn Ezra's reading of צורתם and Radak's alternative 'their strength' recorded in the note.

agent_notes: 'Take me' (יקחני) is the verb used of Enoch (Gen 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kgs 2:3, 5); Meiri and Ibn Ezra cite Genesis 5:24. Whether the psalm expects an afterlife with God or only deliverance from Sheol's power is disputed. Radak glosses כי יקחני as 'for he will make me die', the opposite of the others. I keep the Hebrew's verb and leave the question open in the dramatic layer.

agent_notes: Verse 19 is syntactically ambiguous: 'for he blessed his soul in his life' may be a concession ('though … he blessed himself', KJV, ASV, Webster) or a ground ('for …'). The subject of ויודך is impersonal ('they praise you'). I keep 'for' (כי) in the literal layer and carry the concessive force in the dramatic layer. Rashi, Radak and Meiri each take the second clause as addressed to the listener, as I do.

agent_notes: Request addressed: תָּבוֹא is read as 3fs by Ibn Ezra and Radak (the soul of v. 19) and as 2ms by Rashi, Metzudat David and Malbim (the listener). English cannot keep 'it comes' and 'you come' both, so the literal layer gives the 3fs reading and the commentary and note record the 2ms one. The plural יִרְאוּ is read as the fathers (the generation).
The claim that 'generation of his fathers' stands for Sheol and the family tomb is my own reading, not sourced; Rashi takes it as the wicked generation seen in Gehinnom.

agent_notes: ʿăqēbay is read as 'my heels' (KJV, ASV, Rashi, Metzudat David), with the iniquity 'of my heels' meaning wrongs trodden underfoot and thought small. YLT and BBE take it as 'supplanters', from the same root as Jacob's name (ʿāqab); that reading is mentioned in the commentary and not chosen. The literal layer keeps 'heels' because the Hebrew word is the plain body part.

The first word 'āḥ ('brother') is fronted and ambiguous: Ibn Ezra, Rashi, Radak and Meiri all take it as the object of 'ransom' ('no man can ransom a brother'); a few ancient readers emend to 'ak ('surely'), as BBE ('Truly') and YLT's wording suggest. I keep 'brother'. 'Not … cannot' is rendered as an emphatic 'not … ever': the absolute infinitive pādōh intensifies the negation.

Revised per request: Radak (on וחדל לעולם) is placed with the reading where the redemption or the thing itself ceases, which is also the ASV and KJV reading. Rashi (on 49:8, 'חדל הוא לעולם מלפדותו') is kept for the reading where the would-be redeemer gives up. STEPBible glosses וחדל as 'he will cease'; I glossed it 'and it ceases', the subject being ambiguous in Hebrew. The verse is a parenthesis running into verse 10.
